nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; African American novelist, essayist and critic of jazz and American culture
literary_identity: Novelist and essayist; the author of Invisible Man (1952), the most honoured American novel of the post-war decades, and of two collections of essays on literature, music and American identity.
biography: Ralph Waldo Ellison was born in Oklahoma City on 1 March 1913 and named after Ralph Waldo Emerson. He studied music at the Tuskegee Institute in Alabama from 1933, left for New York in 1936, and there met Langston Hughes and Richard Wright, who encouraged him to write reviews and stories; he worked for the Federal Writers' Project and served in the merchant marine during the Second World War. Invisible Man, begun in 1945 and published by Random House in 1952, won the National Book Award in 1953. He held a fellowship at the American Academy in Rome in the mid-1950s, published the essays of Shadow and Act in 1964, taught at Bard, Rutgers and Yale, and held the Albert Schweitzer Chair in the Humanities at New York University from 1970 to 1979. He received the National Medal of Arts in 1985 and published a second collection, Going to the Territory, in 1986. He worked for some forty years on a second novel that he never finished. He died of pancreatic cancer in New York on 16 April 1994; his literary executor John F. Callahan edited his essays (1995), stories (1996) and the novel Juneteenth (1999) from his papers.
literary_profile: Ralph Ellison's reputation rests on one finished novel and two books of essays: Invisible Man fused the African American folk and blues tradition with the techniques of modernist fiction, and the essays argued that Black American culture is central to, not separate from, American culture as a whole.
stylistic_characteristics: A densely allusive, comic and lyrical prose that shifts between registers, from sermon, folk tale and blues to surrealist nightmare; a first-person narrator who reflects on his own telling; essays that move from personal reminiscence to cultural argument, often through jazz.
intellectual_concerns: Race and visibility in American democracy; identity as improvisation; the folk and vernacular sources of art; jazz and the blues as models of discipline and freedom; the American nation as a mixed, unfinished culture.
historical_significance: Ellison stands with Richard Wright and James Baldwin among the defining African American writers of the mid-twentieth century; Invisible Man was voted the most important American novel since the Second World War in a 1965 Book Week poll, and his essays shaped later arguments about the relation between Black culture and American identity.
biographical_uncertainty: Birth year: Wikipedia and the New World Encyclopedia give 1 March 1913; the Gale entries reproduced by Encyclopedia.com give 1914, the year found in many older references. 1913 is recorded here.
bibliographical_notes: Bibliography status, 1946-2000: substantially complete. Recorded as works: Invisible Man (1952), Shadow and Act (1964), Going to the Territory (1986), The Collected Essays of Ralph Ellison (1995, posthumous), Flying Home and Other Stories (1996, posthumous) and Juneteenth (1999, posthumous). Also recorded: Trading Twelves: The Selected Letters of Ralph Ellison and Albert Murray (2000, posthumous for Ellison), edited by Murray and John F. Callahan; Murray, the other correspondent, has no author record. Not individually recorded: uncollected periodical pieces, including the excerpts from the unfinished second novel published in magazines between 1960 and 1977, are not individually recorded. Outside the period: Living with Music (2002), Three Days Before the Shooting... (2010) and The Selected Letters (2019). Checked against Wikipedia, Encyclopedia.com (Gale) and the New World Encyclopedia.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; British poet, novelist, jazz critic and university librarian
literary_identity: Poet, novelist and librarian; the most widely read English poet of the post-war decades and the central poet of the Movement of the 1950s.
biography: Philip Arthur Larkin was born in Coventry on 9 August 1922 and read English at St John's College, Oxford, where he began a lifelong friendship with Kingsley Amis. He became a librarian, first at Wellington in Shropshire, then as assistant librarian at University College, Leicester, from 1946, sub-librarian at Queen's University, Belfast, from 1950, and from March 1955 Librarian of the University of Hull, the post he held for the rest of his life. His first book of poems, The North Ship (1945), was followed by two novels, Jill (1946) and A Girl in Winter (1947). After a privately printed pamphlet, XX Poems (1951), The Less Deceived (1955) made his reputation, and The Whitsun Weddings (1964) and High Windows (1974) confirmed him as the leading English poet of his generation. He reviewed jazz records for the Daily Telegraph, edited The Oxford Book of Twentieth-Century English Verse (1973) and chaired the Booker Prize judges in 1977. He died of cancer in Hull on 2 December 1985. His Collected Poems (1988), Selected Letters (1992) and Andrew Motion's biography (1993) transformed his posthumous reputation.
literary_profile: Larkin's reputation rests on three mature collections of formally exact, colloquial and ironic poems about ordinary lives, love, ageing and death, together with two early novels, jazz criticism and a small body of essays.
stylistic_characteristics: Traditional stanzas and rhyme handled with conversational ease; plain, precise diction that rises in closing lines to lyrical or visionary images; irony, self-deprecation and bleak comedy; the persona of an unillusioned provincial observer.
intellectual_concerns: Mortality and the fear of death; the gap between expectation and experience; love, marriage and solitude; time and ageing; English towns, landscape and customs; the decline of religious belief and what might replace it.
historical_significance: Larkin is widely regarded as the foremost English poet of the second half of the twentieth century. His rejection of modernist difficulty in favour of a tradition descending from Thomas Hardy shaped the Movement and much later British poetry, while the posthumous letters and biography opened a lasting debate about his views on race and women.
bibliographical_notes: Bibliography status, 1946-2000: substantially complete. Recorded as works: Jill (1946), A Girl in Winter (1947), XX Poems (1951), The Less Deceived (1955), The Whitsun Weddings (1964), All What Jazz (1970), The Oxford Book of Twentieth-Century English Verse (1973, editor), High Windows (1974), Aubade (1977), Required Writing (1983), Collected Poems (1988, posthumous) and Selected Letters of Philip Larkin, 1940-1985 (1992, posthumous). Single poems recorded as selections of The Norton Anthology of English Literature (wave 13): Church Going (1955), MCMXIV and Talking in Bed (1964), Homage to a Government (1969), This Be The Verse (1971), Going, Going (1972), and High Windows (poem), Sad Steps and The Explosion (1974). Not recorded: The Fantasy Poets No. 21 (Fantasy Press, 1954), a pamphlet whose contents have not been verified; uncollected reviews, introductions and broadcasts. Outside the period: The North Ship (1945), which belongs to the 1901-1945 window but is not yet in the database; Trouble at Willow Gables and Other Fictions (2002), Letters to Monica (2010) and The Complete Poems (2012). Checked against Wikipedia (via Wikiwand), EBSCO Research Starters, the New World Encyclopedia and the Sogang University Larkin page.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: American; African American playwright, essayist and civil rights activist
literary_identity: Playwright and activist; author of A Raisin in the Sun (1959), the first play by an African American woman to be produced on Broadway.
biography: Lorraine Vivian Hansberry was born in Chicago on 19 May 1930, the youngest child of a prominent African American family. When her father bought a house in the white neighbourhood of Woodlawn, the family faced a hostile reception and a legal battle over racially restrictive covenants that reached the United States Supreme Court, an experience that later shaped A Raisin in the Sun. She studied at the University of Wisconsin from 1948, left in 1950 for New York, and worked as a staff writer and then associate editor on Paul Robeson's newspaper Freedom (1951-53); in 1952 she represented Robeson at a peace congress in Montevideo. She married the songwriter and producer Robert Nemiroff in 1953; they divorced in 1964, though he remained her collaborator and literary executor. A Raisin in the Sun opened on Broadway in March 1959 and won the New York Drama Critics' Circle Award. Her second play, The Sign in Sidney Brustein's Window, opened in 1964. She was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer in 1963 and died in New York on 12 January 1965, aged thirty-four. Nemiroff later adapted To Be Young, Gifted and Black (1969) from her writings and completed and published her last plays.
literary_profile: Hansberry's few finished plays brought working-class African American family life to the centre of the American stage and joined it to a wider politics of civil rights, anti-colonialism, feminism and intellectual commitment.
stylistic_characteristics: Realist family drama with naturalistic, humorous dialogue that carries political argument; vivid, many-sided characters; symbolic objects and gestures; in the later plays a move towards the drama of ideas and fable.
intellectual_concerns: Housing segregation and racial discrimination; the American Dream and its costs; the dignity of working-class Black families; African independence and colonialism; the responsibility of intellectuals to commit themselves; women's independence.
historical_significance: A Raisin in the Sun is ranked among the classics of American drama and opened Broadway to Black playwrights, directors and audiences; Hansberry's essays, letters and late plays have made her an important figure in the histories of the civil rights movement, Black feminism and lesbian writing.
biographical_uncertainty: Her letters to the lesbian magazine The Ladder in the late 1950s were published anonymously and attributed to her later; the AmericanLiterature.com profile reports them, and the attribution is widely accepted.
bibliographical_notes: Bibliography status, 1946-2000: substantially complete for plays and books. Recorded as works: A Raisin in the Sun (1959), The Sign in Sidney Brustein's Window (staged 1964, published 1965), The Movement: Documentary of a Struggle for Equality (1964), To Be Young, Gifted and Black (1969, adapted by Robert Nemiroff), Les Blancs (staged 1970, completed by Nemiroff), The Drinking Gourd (written 1960) and What Use Are Flowers? (both published posthumously in 1972). Not individually recorded: her journalism for Freedom (1951-55); essays and speeches such as 'On Summer' and 'The Negro Writer and His Roots'; her screenplay for the 1961 film of A Raisin in the Sun; letters published anonymously in The Ladder in the late 1950s; unfinished works. Checked against Britannica, Gale (via Encyclopedia.com) and other references listed with each record.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Trinidadian; Indo-Trinidadian Caribbean (West Indian) novelist, short-story writer and playwright writing in English, of Indian and Scottish-Indian descent, in England from 1950 to 1978 and in Canada from 1978
literary_identity: Trinidad-born novelist whose The Lonely Londoners (1956), narrated as well as spoken in Trinidadian creole, founded the fiction of Caribbean migrant London, and whose novels of Indo-Trinidadian village life, from A Brighter Sun (1952) to The Plains of Caroni (1970), trace the meeting of Indian and Creole Trinidad.
biography: Samuel Dickson Selvon, known as Sam Selvon, was born on 20 May 1923 in San Fernando, in the south of Trinidad, the sixth of seven children. His father, Bertwyn Fraser Selvon, was a Christian of Madrasi Indian descent who managed a dry-goods store; his mother, Daisy Irene Dickson, was the daughter of a Scotsman and of Keasoo, a woman of South Asian origin. Peepal Tree Press, drawing on his own accounts, describes a creolised household with little part in Hindu ritual, and a boy formed by the American films at the local cinemas. He left Naparima College at fifteen and from 1940 to 1945 was a wireless operator with the Trinidad branch of the Royal Naval Reserve (Dawes calls him a telegraph operator), the post that brought him into contact with the wartime American presence. From 1945 (1946 in Britannica) to 1950 he worked for the Trinidad Guardian as a reporter and on its literary page, South Asian Britain says as literary editor of the Sunday Guardian, publishing stories and sketches under the names Michael Wentworth, Esses, Ack-Ack and Big Buffer. He married Draupadi Persaud in 1947. In 1950 he moved to London, where he lived first in a hostel near Earl's Court, took menial jobs and became a clerk at the Indian Embassy, while reading for the BBC's Caribbean Voices and placing stories and poems in the London Magazine, the New Statesman and The Nation. Guggenheim Fellowships (1955 and 1968 in Wikipedia; 1954 and 1968 in Dawes), a Society of Authors travelling scholarship (1958) and Arts Council grants (1960) supported his work, and in 1969 Trinidad and Tobago awarded him the Hummingbird Medal (Gold). He wrote more than twenty radio plays and several television scripts for the BBC, scripted Horace Ové's Pressure (1976), the first full-length Black British feature film, and in the late 1960s took part in the Caribbean Artists Movement. In 1963 he married Althea Daroux. After a creative writing fellowship at the University of Dundee (1975-77) he moved in 1978 to Canada and settled in Calgary, Alberta; he taught creative writing as a visiting professor at the University of Victoria, worked for some months as a janitor at the University of Calgary and then became its writer-in-residence, and Dawes adds residencies at Alberta and Winnipeg. The University of the West Indies (1985) and Warwick (1989) gave him honorary doctorates. He died of respiratory failure on 16 April 1994 during a visit to Trinidad, at Piarco International Airport according to Wikipedia (Britannica says Port of Spain), and received the Chaconia Medal (Gold) posthumously that year.
literary_profile: Selvon published ten novels between 1952 and 1983 (Peepal Tree and Dawes count eleven), one collection of stories, two books of plays and a selection of prose. Six of the novels are set in Trinidad, mostly among Indo-Trinidadians: A Brighter Sun (1952) and its sequel Turn Again Tiger (1958), An Island Is a World (1955), I Hear Thunder (1963), The Plains of Caroni (1970) and Those Who Eat the Cascadura (1972). The others follow West Indians in London: The Lonely Londoners (1956), The Housing Lark (1965) and the two later Moses novels, Moses Ascending (1975) and Moses Migrating (1983); the stories of Ways of Sunlight (1957) move between the two settings. Much of his drama was written for the BBC, and two collections, Eldorado West One (1988) and Highway in the Sun (1991), preserve some of it; Foreday Morning (1989) gathers prose from 1946 onwards.
stylistic_characteristics: In The Lonely Londoners Selvon used creolised English, or 'nation language', for narration as well as dialogue, an innovation Wikipedia calls groundbreaking; he explained that the novel 'just shot along' once he wrote both in dialect. Dawes praises folk idioms of 'sophistication and sheer virtuosity', a rare union of empathy and humour, and a Lonely Londoners told like a 'ballad' or calypso. Schwarz finds in Selvon's London an exact geography and an echo of Eliot's 'unreal' city, and Britannica singles out the 'extensive and striking use of dialect' in Turn Again Tiger.
intellectual_concerns: Creolisation and the relations of Indian and African Trinidadians; the peasant culture of the cane fields and its passing under mechanisation; manhood, marriage and domestic violence; migration to Britain, racism, poverty and the improvised community of 'the boys'; return, Anglophilia and the divided loyalties of the migrant; Carnival as a fleeting image of a society beyond race.
historical_significance: Selvon came to attention in the 1950s with other Caribbean writers, Naipaul among them (Britannica), and is a founder of Caribbean migrant fiction in Britain. The Lonely Londoners, his most widely known book, is read as a forerunner of Zadie Smith's White Teeth and Hanif Kureishi's The Buddha of Suburbia, and Dawes finds his influence 'consistently apparent' in the many fiction writers who followed him. Britannica judged A Brighter Sun the first book in which an East Indian author wrote 'with such quiet authority and simple charm' about Indo-Trinidadian life, and it was long a set text on the Caribbean Examinations Council syllabus.
bibliographical_notes: Bibliography status, 1946-2000: substantially complete for books. Recorded as works: the novels A Brighter Sun (1952), An Island Is a World (1955), The Lonely Londoners (1956), Turn Again Tiger (1958), I Hear Thunder (1963), The Housing Lark (1965), The Plains of Caroni (1970), Those Who Eat the Cascadura (1972), Moses Ascending (1975) and Moses Migrating (1983); the stories Ways of Sunlight (1957), with its story 'Waiting for Aunty to Cough' (1957), a selection of The Norton Anthology of English Literature, recorded separately (wave 13); the plays Eldorado West One (1988) and Highway in the Sun and Other Plays (1991); and Foreday Morning: Selected Prose 1946-1986 (1989). Not recorded as works, because their contents were not examined: 'A Meap Story' (1954), listed only in Wikipedia's bibliography, and 'A Drink of Water' (1968), listed only by Dawes, neither of them described anywhere consulted; stories and poems in Trinidad papers (1945-50), on Caribbean Voices and in the London Magazine, New Statesman, The Nation and Evening Standard, including 'Cane is Bitter' (whether it is in Ways of Sunlight was not checked); more than twenty BBC radio plays and the television scripts Anansi the Spider Man and Home, Sweet India, except as collected in the two books of plays; the screenplay of Pressure (1976), written with Horace Ové; the essays 'The West Indian Patchwork' (1955, for the Royal Geographical Society), 'Three into one can't go - East Indian, Trinidadian or West Indian?' (Wasafiri 3.5, 1986, pp. 8-11) and 'Finding West Indian Identity in London' (Kunapipi 9.3, 1987, pp. 34-38; dated 1988 by Schwarz and reprinted in Tiger's Triumph, 1995); a film script of The Lonely Londoners, finished before his death (Dawes); and, unfinished at his death, the novel 'A High of Zero' and an autobiography (Dawes). Outside the period: Poems of Sam Selvon (ed. Kenneth Ramchand, 2012) and Calypso in London (2023). Checked against the list of published works with first publishers in South Asian Britain, Wikipedia's bibliography, Dawes's list of works and Britannica. Discrepancies: Turn Again Tiger is 1958 in South Asian Britain, Dawes and Britannica but 1959 in Wikipedia's list and Caribbean Beat; Ways of Sunlight is 1957 except in Britannica (1958); I Hear Thunder is 1963 except in Britannica (1962); Eldorado West One is 1988 except in Wikipedia's list (1989); the Guggenheim years (1955 or 1954, and 1968); his wartime post (wireless or telegraph operator); his start at the Trinidad Guardian (1945 or 1946); the number of his novels (ten, or eleven in Peepal Tree, Dawes and the Harry Ransom Center inventory cited by Wikipedia); and the place of his death (Piarco International Airport or Port of Spain).

nationality_or_literary_tradition: English; poet and novelist of London (Palmers Green), writing in English
literary_identity: English poet and novelist whose short, deceptively simple poems, often printed with her own drawings, joke and grieve about death, loneliness, faith and doubt; best known for 'Not Waving but Drowning' (1957)
biography: Florence Margaret Smith, known as Stevie Smith, was born on 20 September 1902 at 34 De La Pole Avenue in Kingston upon Hull, the second daughter of Charles Ward Smith, a shipping agent, and Ethel Rahel Spear. Her father's business and marriage failed and he ran away to sea, and when she was three she moved with her mother and sister to 1 Avondale Road, Palmers Green, in north London, where she lived for the rest of her life with her aunt Madge Spear, the 'Lion Aunt'. At five she developed tuberculous peritonitis and spent three years in a sanatorium near Broadstairs; she dated her preoccupation with death from that time. Her mother died when she was sixteen. She was educated at Palmers Green High School, the North London Collegiate School for Girls and Mrs Hoster's Secretarial College, and from 1923 to 1953 was private secretary to Sir Neville Pearson at the publishers Newnes. Her first two novels and her first book of poems, A Good Time Was Had by All (1937), made her name before the war. After retiring from Newnes following a nervous breakdown she gave readings and broadcasts that won her a younger audience; Sylvia Plath wrote to her in 1962 as 'a desperate Smith-addict'. She described herself as a 'lapsed atheist', and her essay 'The Necessity of Not Believing' (1958) was read to the Cambridge Humanist Society. She received the Cholmondeley Award (1966) and the Queen's Gold Medal for Poetry (1969), and died of a brain tumour on 7 March 1971 in Ashburton, Devon. Hugh Whitemore's play Stevie (filmed in 1978 with Glenda Jackson) is based on her life.
literary_profile: Smith wrote three lightly fictionalised novels, Novel on Yellow Paper (1936), Over the Frontier (1938) and The Holiday (1949), and published nine volumes of poems in her lifetime, from A Good Time Was Had by All (1937) through Harold's Leap (1950), Not Waving but Drowning (1957), Selected Poems (1962), The Frog Prince (1966) and The Best Beast (1969); Scorpion and Other Poems (1972) and the Collected Poems (1975) followed her death. Her best-known poem is 'Not Waving but Drowning'.
stylistic_characteristics: Short poems in irregular lines and comic rhymes, borrowing the rhythms of hymns, nursery rhymes and ballads; dramatic monologues and dialogues; deliberate naivety and awkwardness that turn suddenly bleak; her own drawings, often incongruous with the text. Hermione Lee called 'peculiar' the best word for her effects.
intellectual_concerns: Death as friend and release; loneliness and misunderstanding; faith and unbelief, and the Christianity she could neither accept nor leave; human cruelty and war; myth, legend and fairy tale; middle-class English life; women's independence.
historical_significance: A singular voice in twentieth-century English poetry, without school or followers, whose readings in the 1960s won her a new generation of readers. 'Not Waving but Drowning' is among the best-known English poems of the century, and her reputation has grown since her death with new collected editions.
bibliographical_notes: Books, as listed by Wikipedia: the novels Novel on Yellow Paper (1936), Over the Frontier (1938) and The Holiday (1949); the poems A Good Time Was Had by All (1937), Tender Only to One (1938), Mother, What Is Man? (1942), Harold's Leap (1950), Not Waving but Drowning (1957), Selected Poems (1962), The Frog Prince (1966), The Best Beast (1969), Scorpion and Other Poems (1972, posthumous) and Collected Poems (1975, posthumous); Some Are More Human Than Others (1958), Cats in Colour (1959) and Me Again (1984, posthumous). Wikipedia also lists Alone in the Woods (1947), which was not checked. Installment 10, which records only Norton selections, holds 'Our Bog Is Dood' (1950), 'Not Waving but Drowning' (1957) and 'Thoughts About the Person from Porlock' (1962); 'Pretty' is undated and unrecorded. The books have no work records, so the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Welsh; poet, short-story writer and broadcaster writing in English
literary_identity: Welsh poet and writer of richly rhythmic, image-dense lyrics, of the stories of Portrait of the Artist as a Young Dog and of the 'play for voices' Under Milk Wood, whose readings and broadcasts made him the most popular poet of his day
biography: Dylan Marlais Thomas was born on 27 October 1914 at 5 Cwmdonkin Drive, Swansea, the son of Florence Williams, a seamstress, and David John Thomas, a grammar-school English master with a first-class degree from Aberystwyth; both parents spoke Welsh as well as English. He left school in 1932 to work as a reporter on the South Wales Daily Post. Of the some two hundred poems he wrote between 1931 and 1935, a number were printed while he was still a teenager, beginning in May 1933 with 'And death shall have no dominion'. In London he met Caitlin Macnamara, whom he married in 1937; they had three children. Finding it hard to live by writing, he added reading tours and radio work; his BBC broadcasts of the late 1940s brought him a wide public. His reading tours of the United States in the 1950s made him famous while his drinking and erratic behaviour worsened. On his fourth visit to New York, in 1953, he fell into a coma and died on 9 November 1953, aged thirty-nine; he is buried at St Martin's churchyard, Laugharne.
literary_profile: Thomas's poems were collected in 18 Poems (1934), Twenty-five Poems (1936), The Map of Love (1939), Deaths and Entrances (1946), In Country Sleep (1952) and Collected Poems, 1934-1952 (1952); his prose includes Portrait of the Artist as a Young Dog (1940) and A Child's Christmas in Wales, and his radio play Under Milk Wood was produced after his death.
stylistic_characteristics: Dense, incantatory verse built on sound, rhythm and paradoxical imagery, often in strict and intricate forms (the villanelle of 'Do not go gentle', the syllabic and rhyming patterns of the later poems); biblical cadence; a celebratory, elegiac lyricism.
intellectual_concerns: Birth, sex and death as one process; childhood and the Welsh landscape; time and mortality; religious imagery without orthodox belief; the poet's vocation.
historical_significance: One of the most popular poets of the twentieth century in Britain and America, whose recordings and readings changed the public life of poetry; criticism since his centenary editions has emphasised his modernist poetics over the legend of the 'roistering, drunken and doomed poet'.
bibliographical_notes: Installment 10 records only his Norton selection first published in the period, 'Do not go gentle into that good night' (1951; collected in In Country Sleep and Collected Poems, 1934-1952, both 1952). His other Norton poems were first printed before 1946 and are not recorded. Books (Wikipedia and general knowledge, not checked title by title): 18 Poems (1934), Twenty-five Poems (1936), The Map of Love (1939), Portrait of the Artist as a Young Dog (1940), Deaths and Entrances (1946), In Country Sleep (1952), Collected Poems, 1934-1952 (1952), and, posthumously, Under Milk Wood (1954) and A Child's Christmas in Wales. None has a work record, so the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Jamaican; poet, folklorist, actress and broadcaster writing and performing in Jamaican Creole (Patois), later resident in Canada
literary_identity: Jamaican poet, folklorist and performer, 'Miss Lou', whose comic monologues and poems in Jamaican Creole established the local language as a medium of literature
biography: Louise Simone Bennett was born on 7 September 1919 on North Street in Kingston, Jamaica, the only child of Augustus Cornelius Bennett, who owned a bakery in Spanish Town, and Kerene Robinson, a dressmaker; after her father's death in 1926 she was raised mainly by her mother. She was educated in Kingston and in 1943 studied Jamaican folklore at Friends College, Highgate; that year her poems first appeared in the Sunday Gleaner. In 1945 a British Council scholarship made her the first black student at the Royal Academy of Dramatic Art in London; she worked in repertory and revue in England and presented the BBC programmes Caribbean Carnival (1945-1946) and West Indian Night (1950). Back in Jamaica she worked for the Jamaica Social Welfare Commission (1955-1959), taught folklore and drama at the University of the West Indies, produced the radio monologues Miss Lou's Views (1965-1982) and hosted the children's television programme Ring Ding (1970-1982). She married the theatre promoter Eric Winston Coverley in 1954. She later lived in Scarborough, Ontario, and died in Toronto in July 2006; she lay in state in Kingston and was buried in National Heroes Park.
literary_profile: Bennett's poems and stories were published in Anancy Stories and Poems in Dialect (1944), Laugh with Louise (1961), Jamaica Labrish (1966), Selected Poems (1982) and Aunty Roachy Seh (1993); she also made many recordings of Jamaican folk songs and of her radio and television work.
stylistic_characteristics: Dramatic monologues and conversational poems in Jamaican Creole, usually in ballad quatrains, addressed to a listener such as 'Miss Mattie'; comic irony, proverb and wordplay drawn from the mento and folk traditions; written to be performed.
intellectual_concerns: Jamaican language and identity; colonialism and its reversals; migration; the pretensions of the colour and class hierarchy; the everyday lives of working-class Jamaican women; independence and national culture.
historical_significance: A founding figure of Caribbean poetry in nation language, credited by Linton Kwesi Johnson, Mutabaruka and others; she received the MBE (1960), the Order of Jamaica (1974), the Musgrave Medal (1978) and the Jamaican Order of Merit (2001).
bibliographical_notes: Books (Wikipedia's selected publications): Anancy Stories and Poems in Dialect (1944), Laugh with Louise (1961), Jamaica Labrish (1966), Selected Poems (1982) and Aunty Roachy Seh (1993), with recordings from Jamaican Folk Songs (1954) onwards. Installment 10, which records only Norton selections, holds 'Colonization in Reverse' (Jamaica Labrish, 1966). Her other three Norton selections ('Jamaica Language', 'Dry-Foot Bwoy', 'Jamaica Oman') are not yet dated and not recorded, and the books have no work records, so the bibliography is incomplete.

nationality_or_literary_tradition: Barbadian; Caribbean poet, historian and critic writing in English and nation language, who worked in Ghana, Jamaica, Britain and the United States
literary_identity: Barbadian poet and historian, author of The Arrivants trilogy and of History of the Voice, which made 'nation language' the term for the Caribbean's own English, and inventor of the 'Sycorax video style' of his later books
biography: Lawson Edward Brathwaite was born on 11 May 1930 in Bridgetown, Barbados, to Hilton and Beryl Brathwaite. At Harrison College he started a school newspaper, wrote on jazz and contributed to the magazine Bim; in 1949 he won the Barbados Island Scholarship to Cambridge, where he took a degree in history at Pembroke College in 1953 and began broadcasting poems and stories on the BBC's Caribbean Voices. From 1955 he worked as an education officer in the Gold Coast, witnessing Ghana's independence, which transformed his sense of Caribbean culture; there he married Doris Monica Wellcome (1960) and wrote the play Odale's Choice (1962). He taught in St Lucia and from 1963 in the history department of the University of the West Indies at Mona, Jamaica, co-founded the Caribbean Artists Movement in London in 1966, took his doctorate at Sussex (1968) and launched the journal Savacou in 1971, the year he received the name Kamau in Kenya. After his wife's death in 1986, the destruction of his archive by Hurricane Gilbert in 1988 and a near-fatal attack in Kingston in 1990, his 'time of salt', he became Professor of Comparative Literature at New York University (1992). He won the Neustadt Prize (1994) and the Griffin Poetry Prize (2006), and died in Barbados on 4 February 2020.
literary_profile: His poetry includes the trilogy The Arrivants (1973), gathering Rights of Passage (1967), Masks (1968) and Islands (1969); the second trilogy of Mother Poem (1977), Sun Poem (1982) and X/Self (1987); Middle Passages (1992) and Born to Slow Horses (Griffin Poetry Prize, 2006); his histories and criticism include The Development of Creole Society in Jamaica, 1770-1820 (1971), Contradictory Omens (1974) and History of the Voice (1984).
stylistic_characteristics: Long sequences built from many voices and registers, mixing standard English with nation language; the rhythms of jazz, calypso, work song and ritual; typographic experiment, culminating in the 'Sycorax video style' of computer fonts and layouts.
intellectual_concerns: The African diaspora and the Middle Passage; the recovery of African elements in Caribbean culture; creolisation; language, voice and the inheritance of colonial forms; history, catastrophe and survival.
historical_significance: One of the major voices of Caribbean literature and its leading theorist of nation language; The Arrivants is generally considered his best work.
bibliographical_notes: Books (Wikipedia's selected works, not checked title by title): poetry from Rights of Passage (1967), Masks (1968) and Islands (1969), gathered as The Arrivants (1973), through Other Exiles (1975), Black + Blues (1976), Mother Poem (1977), Sun Poem (1982), Third World Poems (1983), X/Self (1987), Shar (1992), Middle Passages (1992), Barabajan Poems (1994), DreamStories (1994), Ancestors (2001) and Born to Slow Horses (dated 2006 by Wikipedia); prose including Folk Culture of the Slaves in Jamaica (1970), The Development of Creole Society in Jamaica, 1770-1820 (1971), Contradictory Omens (1974), History of the Voice (1984) and The Zea Mexican Diary (1993). Installment 10, which records only Norton selections, holds History of the Voice (1984), 'Calypso' (1967) and 'Letter SycoraX' (1992); '[On Sycorax Video Style]' is undated and unrecorded. Doris Monica Brathwaite's EKB: His Published Prose & Poetry, 1948-1986 (1986) was not consulted. The bibliography is incomplete.
